## The question of the paper {#the-question-of-the-paper .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **The question.** Do the officials who control access to a public programme answer people differently by race or ethnicity? Officials who deal with the public directly, and decide how much help to give, are **street-level bureaucrats** [@Lipsky1980StreetLevelBureaucracy]
- **The method.** An **audit study** sends matched requests, or matched applicants, that differ in one characteristic, and compares what comes back [@BertrandMullainathan2004AreEmilyGreg; @Pager2003MarkCriminalRecord]. Here the characteristic is a name
- **What it added.** Audits of politicians and local election officials had found discrimination [@ButlerBroockman2011PoliticiansRaciallyDiscriminate; @WhiteEtAl2015WhatNeedVote]. This one asks about a bureaucracy that hands out a valuable benefit and is less tied to politics
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The paper is an experiment published in 2017 [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. From here on I call its two authors **the original authors (OAs)**.
:::

::: notes
Our case study is a paper in the American Journal of Political Science, and from here on I call its two authors the original authors, because the workshop is about the claim and its analyses rather than about the people who made it. The question is an old and important one, whether the officials who stand between citizens and a public programme answer people differently by race or ethnicity. Following Lipsky, sociologists call such officials street-level bureaucrats, since they deal with the public directly and decide how much help to give. The method is the audit study, which sends matched requests that differ in one characteristic and compares the responses. Earlier audits had found discrimination by politicians and by local election officials, and the original authors asked whether the same holds in a bureaucracy that controls access to something valuable, public housing, and is less tied to politics.
:::

## The design {#the-design .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.small}
- Every public housing authority that could be matched with a core city of a metropolitan or micropolitan area: **1,017** in the paper, **`r format(nrow(housing), big.mark = ",")`** in the public file
- **One email each**, sent on one of two days in the same week of 2014
- Each authority assigned **at random**, "via random number generator", to one of six senders
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.small}
| Names meant to indicate | Male | Female |
|:--|:--|:--|
| a white sender | Brett Smith | Emily Smith |
| a Black sender | Tyrone Johnson | Shanice Johnson |
| a Hispanic sender | Santiago Martinez | Gabriela Martinez |
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
One male and one female name per group, because about three-quarters of the families in public housing are headed by women. The Hispanic names rely on the surname Martinez, nearly 92% of whose bearers are Hispanic; their first names peaked in the 1990s and 2000s, so the ages of the six senders could not be matched.
:::

::: {.src}
@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, accepted manuscript, pp. 8–11.
:::

::: notes
The design is simple. The original authors took every public housing authority in the United States that could be matched with a core city, just over a thousand of them, and sent each one a single email in one week of 2014. Each authority was assigned at random to one of six senders, whose names were meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic sender, a man and a woman in each group, because about three quarters of the families in public housing are headed by women. [advance] Names are an imperfect manipulation. The Hispanic names rely on the surname Martinez, most of whose bearers are Hispanic, and the Hispanic first names peaked in popularity later than the others, so these senders may also have read as younger. We return to that point at the end.
:::

## The email {#the-email}

::: {.claimcard .fs-80}
Hello,

My name is X and I'm trying to figure out how to apply for public housing. I believe I may be eligible.

Can you direct me to information about applying for public housing here? I also heard there might be a wait list for this program. How long is it?

Thanks, X
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Four outcomes were coded from what came back: any reply, a reply within 24 hours, information about the wait list, and the tone – "whether the emailer is addressed by proper name. We were lenient in coding 'yes.' A named salutation could be as causal [sic] as 'Hi Brett' or as formal as 'Dear Ms. Martinez.'"
:::

::: {.src}
@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, accepted manuscript, pp. 10 and 12–14.
:::

::: notes
This is the whole email, word for word, with X standing for the name of the sender. It is short, polite and plausible, written by someone who thinks they may be eligible and asks how to apply and how long the wait list is. Every authority received this text, and only the name at the top and at the bottom differed. [advance] From the replies the original authors coded four outcomes: whether the authority replied at all, whether it replied within a day, whether it gave information about the wait list, and the tone. Tone was measured in one way only, by whether the reply addressed the sender by name, and the coding was lenient, so that "Hi Brett" counts and so does "Dear Ms. Martinez". Our claim is about this last outcome.
:::

## What came back {#what-came-back}

```{r}
#| label: names-chart
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.2
# The six names (data/display_names.csv): the share of delivered emails that
# drew a reply, and the share of replies with a greeting code that opened
# with the name of the sender, each with its 95% Wilson interval.
name_rows <- datawizard::data_filter(names_disp, level == "name")
names_long <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::transmute(name_rows, name, group, measure = "Replied: share of delivered emails",
            pct = reply_pct, lo = reply_lo, hi = reply_hi),
  dplyr::transmute(name_rows, name, group, measure = "Greeted by name: share of coded replies",
            pct = named_pct, lo = named_lo, hi = named_hi)
) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(name = factor(name, levels = rev(name_order)),
                          measure = factor(measure, levels = unique(measure)))

ggplot2::ggplot(names_long, ggplot2::aes(pct, name, colour = group)) +
  ggplot2::geom_linerange(ggplot2::aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), linewidth = 1.1) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 3.8) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ measure) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = group_cols) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(limits = c(25, 75), labels = \(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "per cent, with 95% intervals", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(16) +
  ggplot2::theme(strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", colour = ncl_blue, size = 15),
        panel.spacing.x = ggplot2::unit(2, "lines"),
        axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"))
```

::: {.small}
Each name drew replies to between `r fmt_num(min(name_rows$reply_pct), 1)`% and `r fmt_num(max(name_rows$reply_pct), 1)`% of its delivered emails. Greetings by name ranged from `r fmt_num(min(name_rows$named_pct), 1)`% of the coded replies to Santiago to `r fmt_num(max(name_rows$named_pct), 1)`% of those to Emily.
:::

::: {.src}
data/display_names.csv, from the public file of the OAs: `r format(sum(name_rows$delivered), big.mark = ",")` delivered emails, `r format(sum(name_rows$replies), big.mark = ",")` replies, `r format(sum(name_rows$coded), big.mark = ",")` with a greeting code.
:::

::: notes
Here is what came back for each name in the public file. The left panel gives the share of delivered emails that drew any reply, and the six names sit close together, between fifty-two and sixty-three per cent, with heavily overlapping intervals. The right panel gives the share of replies that opened with the name of the sender, and there the picture changes. The white names and Tyrone are at about sixty per cent and Shanice at fifty-two, while the two Hispanic names, in burgundy, sit well to the left, Gabriela at forty-six per cent and Santiago at thirty-seven. The replies came at similar rates, then, and what differed was how they began. The two panels also have different denominators, since the left counts delivered emails and the right only the replies, a difference to which we come back later.
:::

## Four outcomes {#four-outcomes}

```{r}
#| label: outcomes-chart
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.9
# Four outcomes (data/display_outcomes.csv), each compared for the Hispanic
# and for the Black names with the white names: the difference in points,
# with its 95% interval from the HC2 standard error.
outcome_labels <- c(reply = "Any reply\n(delivered emails)",
                    reply24 = "Reply within 24 hours\n(replies)",
                    named = "Greeted by name\n(coded replies)",
                    named_any = "Greeted by name\n(delivered emails)")
outcomes |>
  datawizard::data_modify(outcome = factor(outcome_labels[outcome], levels = rev(outcome_labels)),
                          contrast = factor(contrast, levels = c("black", "hispanic"))) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(b_pp, outcome, colour = contrast)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = grey_mid) +
  ggplot2::geom_linerange(ggplot2::aes(xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high),
                          linewidth = 1.1, position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.55)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 3.6, position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.55)) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(hispanic = burgundy, black = "#4a78ab"),
                      labels = c(hispanic = "Hispanic names", black = "Black names"),
                      breaks = c("hispanic", "black"), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) fmt_num(x, 0)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "difference from the white names (percentage points), with 95% intervals", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(15) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "right",
        legend.margin = ggplot2::margin(0, 0, -6, 0), axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"))
```

::: {.small}
Black names drew replies about as often as white names (`r fmt_signed(out_of("reply", "black", "b_pp"), 1)` points), Hispanic names `r fmt_num(abs(out_of("reply", "hispanic", "b_pp")), 1)` points less often (`r fmt_p(out_of("reply", "hispanic", "p"))`, two-sided; the paper reports p = .11, one-tailed). The large gap is in the greeting: `r fmt_num(out_of("named", "hispanic", "b_pp"), 1)` points among the coded replies.
:::

::: notes
The same data appear here as differences from the white names, for four outcomes, with the Black names in blue and the Hispanic names in burgundy. For any reply, the Black names did slightly better than the white names and the Hispanic names slightly worse, and neither difference is distinguishable from zero. The paper reports the Hispanic gap with a p of point one one, which is the one-tailed value of this test, while the two-tailed value is point two one. For a reply within a day there is no clear gap either. Among the replies with a greeting code, however, the Hispanic names were greeted by name twenty points less often, with an interval far from zero. The bottom row counts every delivered email, with no reply counted as no greeting, and there the gap is about thirteen points, a row that becomes important when we draw the causal graph.
:::

## The claim {#the-claim .smaller}

::: {.claimcard}
"Hispanic housing applicants were twenty percentage points less likely to be greeted by name than were their black and white counterparts." <span class="src">the abstract</span>
:::

::: {.fragment .claimcard}
"Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts" <span class="src">the claim as SCORE selected it for the robustness study</span>
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The published result behind it: Table 1, model 3, a logistic regression on the three groups with community controls and the Hard Email indicator – Hispanic name **−0.82** (SE 0.22), p < 0.01, on **549** replies; as a change in the predicted probability of a named greeting, **−20.0 percentage points**, 95% CI −30.5 to −10.0.
:::

::: {.src}
@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, abstract, Table 1 and p. 18 of the accepted manuscript; the record of the claim in the robustness study.
:::

::: notes
This is the sentence of the abstract from which the claim was taken: Hispanic applicants were twenty percentage points less likely to be greeted by name than their Black and white counterparts. [advance] This is the claim as SCORE selected it for the analysts of the robustness study, with two ellipses. The first removes "twenty percentage points", so the claim states a direction without a size. The second removes "their black and", so the claim compares the Hispanic names with the white names only, where the abstract compares them with the Black and white names together. [advance] The published number comes from a logistic regression on the replies with controls for the community, a coefficient of minus point eight two, which the original authors translate into twenty points. There are two versions of one claim, then, and between them the five analysts tested both.
:::
